28/S0/F0.text: The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

28/S0/F1.text: Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

28/S0/F2.text: The interior of the human eye is liquid, so after transmission through the lens light passes through liquid, whereas in an artificially created lens setup light passes through air after the lens.

28/S0/F3.text: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

28/S0/F4.text: Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.

28/S0/F5.text: The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

28/S0/F6.text: A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.

28/S0/F7.text: For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

28/S0/F8.text: In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

28/S1/F0.text: Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

28/S1/F1.text: The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

28/S1/F2.text: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.

28/S1/F3.text: Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space.

28/S1/F4.text: Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

28/S1/F5.text: When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

28/S2/F0.text: A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

28/S2/F1.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

28/S2/F2.text: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

28/S2/F3.text: In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

28/S3/F0.text: Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.

28/S3/F1.text: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

28/S3/F2.text: Aliasing in a display is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible, such as when the display is highly magnified or zoomed out.

28/S3/F3.text: The screen door effect is an effect, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display (LCD) projectors, in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it.

28/S3/F4.text: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display.

28/S3/F5.text: Because augmented reality (AR) experiences are typically experienced using displays at a distance from the eye, the 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion, which is suitable for distant displays such as televisions, laptops, and smartphones, can be taken into account when designing such AR experiences.

28/S3/F6.text: For augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays and virtual reality (VR) headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye, the traditional 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion is not very suitable; a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch (ppi) is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.

28/S3/F7.text: To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

28/S3/F8.text: For motion perception in an immersive environment, temporal resolution in a virtual reality (VR) headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second (fps) or 60 fps, with higher frame rates preferred.
